PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

Proposition 38
Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi-Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures-Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)-giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see "Overview of State Bond Debt" later in this guide.
Proposal
New Bond for Specified Medical Research. Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body's immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.
Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
Requires Purchases From California Suppliers. Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
Requires California Patient Discount. Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.
Fiscal Effects
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years . The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries. The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state's bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the medical research bond. The state could recover part or all of this cost in subsequent decades if the funded research leads to discoveries that generate revenue.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue.

This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.

And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.

This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it?
by
Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/)
July 31, 2026 Updated August 3, 2026
Republish

Immunology professor Dr. Ruchi Srivastava works in a lab at UC Irvine in Irvine on Feb. 3, 2021. Photo by Leonard Ortiz, Orange County Register via Getty Images
In summary
Proposition 38 is written in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It will appear on the November ballot as Proposition 38 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf), which would provide $8.4 billion for cutting edge immunology research and cures for heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer’s, as well as other diseases that may be vanquished with immunotherapies.
Included in that is more than $4 billion for one, unnamed institute. The legal language behind the proposition gives no outward indication where that $4 billion would go other than pages of oddly specific language that outlines the parameters the lucky recipient must meet to qualify for the windfall.
That might not mean much to the average voter who is trying to parse 14 propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) as they fill out their ballots.
But a CalMatters analysis shows that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition.
The analysis raises the question of why the framers took such care to construct a highly specific set of criteria that seemingly points to a single eligible institute without naming it in the bond.
READ NEXT
He spent decades researching dementia. Trump’s DEI purge killed his grant, and dozens more (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2025/04/health-research/)
April 10, 2025 April 10, 2025
“It is very clearly designed to support a specific nonprofit,” said Sarah Hill, a professor of political science at Cal State Fullerton who studies California’s ballot process. She said Prop. 38’s language is “oddly specific with numbers,” which on its own should raise the suspicion of voters.
“Why is it just this one institute that you have designated that’s going to get half the money?” she asked, posing a question she believes voters too will wonder.
The split design of the bond measure might also trouble voters, Hill added. As written, the bond measure would mete out more than $4 billion to one unnamed institute and over $4 billion to select nonprofit and public university researchers who apply for grants on a competitive basis.
It’s as if the bond backers are saying, “it’s OK that some of it is going to a specific nonprofit because the rest is much broader, much more general,” Hill said. “They’re trying to get people to focus there, but would half of the money still be designated for one nonprofit? Essentially, yes.”
Hill doesn’t know why the bond measure’s backers are hopeful it’ll pass. One possible reason she gave: Enough voters won’t scrutinize this thoroughly and they’ll support it because it promotes medical research into recognizable diseases.
“They’re hoping the way this goes, the voters will just think it sounds nice, which sometimes works,” she added.
There’s recent history that a confusing ballot measure targeting just one entity passes, albeit barely. In 2024 voters approved Proposition 34 by 50.9%. It placed limits on how health care providers spend money. Never explicitly mentioned in the measure’s text was that it appeared to apply to only one organization (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/11/california-election-results-prop-34-health-care-spending/): the AIDS Healthcare Foundation.

Backer of bond is also co-founder of immunology institute
The billionaire (https://www.forbes.com/profile/gary-michelson/) co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, Gary K. Michelson, is one of the two ultrawealthy chief backers of Proposition 38 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf). The institute first became a nonprofit in 2022. Michelson has given it at least $120 million since then. Michelson is the board chair of the institute, which is housed at a research center owned by UCLA (https://www3.research.ucla.edu/research-park).
Prop. 38’s language allocates half the bond money to one unnamed nonprofit that must meet very specific criteria:
It’s a nonprofit founded before 2025;
It focuses on immunology and immunotherapy research rather than research broadly;
It’s affiliated with a University of California campus with a medical center that serves a minimum number of patients. Currently only UCLA meets that threshold;
It must meet a minimum square footage requirement for the size of the research institute;
It received a minimum dollar amount in donations from funders, including for specific research endeavors.
A UCLA spokesperson, Phil Hampton, confirmed that among all nonprofit entities affiliated with UCLA, only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy could satisfy the stipulations of Prop. 38.
The website (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) supporting the proposition touts it as an effort to award grant dollars to scientists working on drug therapies for incurable diseases, but makes no mention of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy as a likely recipient of half the bond revenue. Michelson and a nonprofit that he founded, the Michelson Center For Public Policy, donated (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1485847&view=late1) at least $8.2 million to the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign. Another campaign donor and institute co-founder, Meyer Luskin, has given (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1485847&view=late1) at least $5 million.
A former science research administrator publicly opposes the proposition. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federally funded National Institutes of Health — the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research. He said concentrating half the funding to one unnamed institute is unfair. “There is a lot of talent in immunology, immunotherapy research in California,” he said in an interview. “All the institutions are scrambling, and so tracking a huge portion of it to one institution, I think, is a bad idea.”
Kaplan also worries the bond measure is too focused on one discipline —immunotherapy — at theexpense of a wider array of biomedical research (https://amp.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article315629674.html). He’s currently a senior scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine’s Clinical Excellence Research Center.
The Michelson Center for Public Policy, where Michelson is the director, has given (https://calmatters.org/about/funding/#:~:text=Michelson%20Center%20for%20Public%20Policy) between $1,000 and $9,900 to CalMatters.
The potential for cures through immunotherapies is huge because most diseases involve the immune system, the bond measure backers say. California science research has been rocked by funding cuts ordered by the White House that led to hundreds of cancelled federal grants. While many of those grants were restored (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/), the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign says ongoing federal funding instability necessitates state investment in immunology and immunotherapies.
Should Prop. 38 pass, bond payments will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250488.pdf), bringing the cost of the $8.4 billion bond to more than $12 billion, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The office said costs to the state may be less if the drug therapies developed through the bond’s research funding generate profits that are then routed back to California’s coffers.
What bond backer says
CalMatters presented its findings to the The Yes on 38 (https://yeson38.com/) campaign. In a lengthy email response, Claudia Briggs, the campaign’s spokesperson, said Prop. 38’s language isn’t uniquely tailored to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. She defended the detailed eligibility criteria written into the bond proposition.
“We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding,” she wrote. “We can’t speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify across California.”
Briggs wrote that the eligibility criteria were “intentionally designed to ensure that whichever institute is selected is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
She explained that the eligibility criteria were crafted to “ensure the selected institute is primarily focused on immunology and immunotherapy research, already has significant resources before receiving bond funds, has an adequate physical facility to accommodate multiple labs and research programs, and has an existing close working relationship with at least one UC campus in order to establish the foundation for the cross-collaboration that will be important to the success of the measure.”
Drugs created through research funded by the bond would have to be discounted at 20% for California residents and 10% of any revenue from the drugs developed through bond-funded research would go back to the state’s general fund. If the revenues repay what the state spent on the bond and there’s money left over (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=13), the spare cash would return to the special account supporting the goals of the bond.
The bond measure language says that if no institute qualifies, the California Department of Public Health can adjust the criteria to select a winning institute.
How the bond seemingly points to one institute
The bond proposition language says that the institute receiving the $4.2 billion must be affiliated with a University of California campus housing a medical center with more than 3.5 million outpatient visitors and at least 35,000 inpatient admissions.
According to the UC’s latest fiscal audit (https://www.ucop.edu/uc-controller/financial-reports/systemwide-reports/medical-center-reports/24-25/medical-center-report-2025.pdf#page=30), only the UCLA medical center and its affiliated sites registered more than 3.5 million outpatient visits in 2025, with 4.1 million visits. UC San Francisco came in second with 3.4 million visits. UCLA’s website says its medical system admits at least 46,000 people for inpatient care (https://www.uclahealth.org/discover/about).
Based on that criteria, only an institute affiliated with UCLA is presently eligible for the $4.2 billion fund.
The bond measure also requires that the research entity measures at least 200,000 square feet and has a “primary” purpose of “conducting research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy.” Press releases (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/michelsons-give-120-million-gift-to-ucla-immunology-immunotherapy) from 2024indicate (https://www.michelsonmedicalresearch.org/news/california-institute-for-immunology-and-immunotherapy-new-ucla-research-park) that the institute will occupy between 360,000 and 500,000 square feet of space on UCLA-owned property.
The institute’s stated purpose is to be an (https://www.calimmunology.org/) “invention factory” for “life-saving drugs, vaccines, diagnostics” and to “end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” It initially received (https://www.michelsonmedicalresearch.org/news/ucla-receives-120-million-gift-from-alya-and-gary-michelson-ciii#:~:text=%24200%20million%20appropriation%20from%20the%20state%20of%20California) $200 million in support from the state budget that helped to secure (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/california-legislature-first-day/#:~:text=In%20other%20higher%20education%20news%3A) the UCLA research space.
One of the other requirements of Prop. 38 is that the nonprofit receiving the $4.2 billion be an entity that’s received at least $250 million in philanthropic support. The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy has received a reported $250 million (https://labusinessjournal.com/special-reports/bioscience-institute-takes-shape/#:~:text=Private%20donation%20commitments%20have%20totaled%20%24250%20million%20to%20date%2C%20primarily%20from%20the%20six%2Dmember%20board.).
Another bond measure requirement is that top officials from the affiliated UC campus sit on the unnamed institute’s board (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=7). Four top UCLA administrators are listed on the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy’s board of directors, including the campus chancellor, Julio Frenk, and the school’s vice chancellor for research, Roger Wakimoto. The institute’s webpage, labeled “Board of Directors,” lists the senior UCLA personnel as “UCLA Board of Directors.” At least four UCLA officials must sit on the institute’s fiduciary board, according to a 2023 term sheet (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/aug23/h3attach1.pdf#page=3)of the affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute. The UCLA personnel are named as directors in the institute’s most recent Form 990 tax filing (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093/202631219349301013/full).
Prop. 38 is highly specific about two donations that must be at least $50 million each that seem to only apply to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The bond language says one donation is to support “a rapid vaccine development program” and the other supports “a microbiome research program.”
Michelson and his wife donated $50 million to two research programs with near-verbatim descriptions that match the bond language as part of their $120 million contribution to the institute, according toa press release (https://www.garykmichelson.org/blog/ucla-receives-120-million-gift-from-alya-and-gary-michelson-for-new-california-institute-for-immunology-amp-immunotherapy). The microbiome research will be conducted in collaboration with the UCLA Goodman-Luskin Microbiome Center, which Luskin and his wife helped establish through a $20 million donation they made with another couple (https://www.uclahealth.org/news/release/ucla-receives-20-million-establish-goodman-luskin-microbiome).
Other grants limited to select researchers
While an unnamed institute is to receive half the money from Prop. 38, the other half will be meted out to a narrow array of public and nonprofit-based researchers in California through a competitive grant application process.
A council selected by the chancellors of seven of the 10 UC campuses, officials from other universities and nonprofit researchers will select the winning grant proposals (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=10). The three UC

This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it?

By Mikhail Zinshteyn, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

It will appear on the November ballot as Proposition 38, which would provide $8.4 billion for cutting edge immunology research and cures for heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer’s, as well as other diseases that may be vanquished with immunotherapies.

Included in that is more than $4 billion for one, unnamed institute. The legal language behind the proposition gives no outward indication where that $4 billion would go other than pages of oddly specific language that outlines the parameters the lucky recipient must meet to qualify for the windfall.

That might not mean much to the average voter who is trying to parse 14 propositions as they fill out their ballots.

But a CalMatters analysis shows that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition.

The analysis raises the question of why the framers took such care to construct a highly specific set of criteria that seemingly points to a single eligible institute without naming it in the bond.

“It is very clearly designed to support a specific nonprofit,” said Sarah Hill, a professor of political science at Cal State Fullerton who studies California’s ballot process. She said Prop. 38’s language is “oddly specific with numbers,” which on its own should raise the suspicion of voters.

“Why is it just this one institute that you have designated that's going to get half the money?” she asked, posing a question she believes voters too will wonder.

The split design of the bond measure might also trouble voters, Hill added. As written, the bond measure would mete out more than $4 billion to one unnamed institute and over $4 billion to select nonprofit and public university researchers who apply for grants on a competitive basis. 

It’s as if the bond backers are saying, “it's OK that some of it is going to a specific nonprofit because the rest is much broader, much more general,” Hill said. “They're trying to get people to focus there, but would half of the money still be designated for one nonprofit? Essentially, yes.”

Hill doesn’t know why the bond measure’s backers are hopeful it’ll pass. One possible reason she gave: Enough voters won’t scrutinize this thoroughly and they’ll support it because it promotes medical research into recognizable diseases. 

“They're hoping the way this goes, the voters will just think it sounds nice, which sometimes works,” she added.

There’s recent history that a confusing ballot measure targeting just one entity passes, albeit barely. In 2024 voters approved Proposition 34 by 50.9%. It placed limits on how health care providers spend money. Never explicitly mentioned in the measure’s text was that it appeared to apply to only one organization: the AIDS Healthcare Foundation.

Backer of bond is also co-founder of immunology institute

The billionaire co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, Gary K. Michelson, is one of the two ultrawealthy chief backers of Proposition 38. The institute first became a nonprofit in 2022. Michelson has given it at least $120 million since then. Michelson is the board chair of the institute, which is housed at a research center owned by UCLA. 

Prop. 38’s language allocates half the bond money to one unnamed nonprofit that must meet very specific criteria: 

  • It’s a nonprofit founded before 2025;
  • It focuses on immunology and immunotherapy research rather than research broadly;
  • It’s affiliated with a University of California campus with a medical center that serves a minimum number of patients. Currently only UCLA meets that threshold; 
  • It must meet a minimum square footage requirement for the size of the research institute;
  • It received a minimum dollar amount in donations from funders, including for specific research endeavors. 

A UCLA spokesperson, Phil Hampton, confirmed that among all nonprofit entities affiliated with UCLA, only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy could satisfy the stipulations of Prop. 38. 

The website supporting the proposition touts it as an effort to award grant dollars to scientists working on drug therapies for incurable diseases, but makes no mention of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy as a likely recipient of half the bond revenue. Michelson and a nonprofit that he founded, the Michelson Center For Public Policy, donated at least $8.2 million to the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign. Another campaign donor and institute co-founder, Meyer Luskin, has given at least $5 million.

A former science research administrator publicly opposes the proposition. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federally funded National Institutes of Health — the world's largest public funder of biomedical research. He said concentrating half the funding to one unnamed institute is unfair. "There is a lot of talent in immunology, immunotherapy research in California," he said in an interview. "All the institutions are scrambling, and so tracking a huge portion of it to one institution, I think, is a bad idea." 

Kaplan also worries the bond measure is too focused on one discipline —immunotherapy — at the expense of a wider array of biomedical research. He's currently a senior scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine’s Clinical Excellence Research Center.

The Michelson Center for Public Policy, where Michelson is the director, has given between $1,000 and $9,900 to CalMatters.

The potential for cures through immunotherapies is huge because most diseases involve the immune system, the bond measure backers say. California science research has been rocked by funding cuts ordered by the White House that led to hundreds of cancelled federal grants. While many of those grants were restored, the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign says ongoing federal funding instability necessitates state investment in immunology and immunotherapies.

Should Prop. 38 pass, bond payments will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years, bringing the cost of the $8.4 billion bond to more than $12 billion, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The office said costs to the state may be less if the drug therapies developed through the bond’s research funding generate profits that are then routed back to California’s coffers.

What bond backer says

CalMatters presented its findings to the The Yes on 38 campaign. In a lengthy email response, Claudia Briggs, the campaign’s spokesperson, said Prop. 38’s language isn’t uniquely tailored to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. She defended the detailed eligibility criteria written into the bond proposition.

“We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding,” she wrote. “We can’t speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify across California.”

Briggs wrote that the eligibility criteria were “intentionally designed to ensure that whichever institute is selected is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”

She explained that the eligibility criteria were crafted to “ensure the selected institute is primarily focused on immunology and immunotherapy research, already has significant resources before receiving bond funds, has an adequate physical facility to accommodate multiple labs and research programs, and has an existing close working relationship with at least one UC campus in order to establish the foundation for the cross-collaboration that will be important to the success of the measure.”

Drugs created through research funded by the bond would have to be discounted at 20% for California residents and 10% of any revenue from the drugs developed through bond-funded research would go back to the state’s general fund. If the revenues repay what the state spent on the bond and there’s money left over, the spare cash would return to the special account supporting the goals of the bond. 

The bond measure language says that if no institute qualifies, the California Department of Public Health can adjust the criteria to select a winning institute. 

How the bond seemingly points to one institute

The bond proposition language says that the institute receiving the $4.2 billion must be affiliated with a University of California campus housing a medical center with more than 3.5 million outpatient visitors and at least 35,000 inpatient admissions.

According to the UC’s latest fiscal audit, only the UCLA medical center and its affiliated sites registered more than 3.5 million outpatient visits in 2025, with 4.1 million visits. UC San Francisco came in second with 3.4 million visits. UCLA’s website says its medical system admits at least 46,000 people for inpatient care.

Based on that criteria, only an institute affiliated with UCLA is presently eligible for the $4.2 billion fund. 

The bond measure also requires that the research entity measures at least 200,000 square feet and has a “primary” purpose of “conducting research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy.” Press releases from 2024 indicate that the institute will occupy between 360,000 and 500,000 square feet of space on UCLA-owned property. 

The institute's stated purpose is to be an “invention factory” for “life-saving drugs, vaccines, diagnostics” and to “end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” It initially received $200 million in support from the state budget that helped to secure the UCLA research space. 

One of the other requirements of Prop. 38 is that the nonprofit receiving the $4.2 billion be an entity that’s received at least $250 million in philanthropic support. The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy has received a reported $250 million.

Read the full measure ↗ (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf)Official voter guide ↗ (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm)
01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.

One more question
Why less sunlight for billions in public money?
Despite promises of accountability, the selected institute would not be treated as a public agency under key California transparency and ethics laws, including the Public Records Act, open-meeting requirements and the Political Reform Act.
Public money should come with full public accountability.
Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. CalMatters reported that its eligibility criteria very likely point to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder and board chair is the largest financial backer of Proposition 38.
What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.
What should California do instead? Use independent scientific review and open competition to fund the strongest proposals across institutions and fields. Research priorities should be able to change as evidence, technology and public-health needs evolve.

enacting this act to achieve all of the following:

This is verified directly in the text. So the institute receiving $4.2 billion in taxpayer bond money would be explicitly exempt from:
- California Public Records Act
- Brown Act (open meetings)
- Political Reform Act (conflict-of-interest / financial disclosure)

And Section 130363(b)(1): "A member of the council shall not make, participate in making, or in any way attempt to use their official position to influence a decision to approve or award a grant or contract to their employer, but a member may participate in a decision to approve or award a grant or contract to an entity in the same field as their employer." — so council members CAN vote grants to entities in the same field as their employer. And (b)(2): "A member of the council may participate in a decision to approve or award a grant or contract to an entity for the purpose of research involving a disease from which the member or a person in their family suffers."

Also Section 130363(d): Section 1090 of the Government Code (the anti-self-dealing statute) shall not apply to grants made by the council except under narrow conditions.

Also verified: Section 130358(e)(2): the institute serves as "a clearinghouse and approval center for ALL agreements to sell, license, or otherwise commercialize or monetize intellectual property rights that arise from research funded under this chapter" — i.e., the single institute controls IP commercialization for all grant recipients too.

Also 130357(d): each grant recipient must offer the institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research" and (e) must offer UCLA the same for clinical trials.

Also 130356(e)(2): "The council shall confer with the institute ... in making final decisions regarding the funding of grant proposals."

Also grants only go to institutions "represented on the council" — 130352(b)(2) — a self-selected closed pool. And the council's first chair is the UCLA representative (130355(d)(2)).

Also 130353(e)(1): $100 million General Fund start-up LOAN to the institute, immediately upon the effective date — before any bonds are sold.

Also eligibility criteria in 130353(a): confirmed exactly as CalMatters reported — >35,000 inpatient admissions and >3,500,000 outpatient visits; ≥200,000 sq ft; ≥$250M philanthropic; ≥$50M for "rapid vaccine development program" and ≥$50M for "microbiome research program"; founded before Jan 1, 2025; affiliation agreement before Jan 1, 2025. These are hyper-specific and match CIII/Michelson/Luskin exactly.

Also note: the "20% below national average price" discount only applies to drugs developed through Prop 38-funded research — a tiny fraction of drugs. So the "20% Rx discount" claim in the pro argument is essentially meaningless to almost all Californians. That's a misleading claim in the ballot argument.

Also the pro argument says "Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers" — but the LAO's official fiscal estimate says $500-600M/year for ~20 years from the General Fund, i.e., ~$10-12B total. The revenue offset is speculative and could "take decades." So "no cost to taxpayers" is contradicted by the state's own nonpartisan analyst. That's a materially false statement in the official rebuttal.

Let me check a couple more things:
1. The AG constitutional challenge
2. LA Times editorial board position
3. Any counter-arguments from scientists supporting it
4. The institute's readiness (3 employees)
5. Compare with Prop 71/14 stem cell bonds track record (CIRM) — did they generate revenue? That's relevant to the "no cost to taxpayers" claim.

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.

This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready
CalMatters (https://laist.com/people/calmatters)
Mikhail Zinshteyn | CalMatters
Published October 20, 2026 at 3:00 PM PDT
Courtyard view of the UCLA Research Park under construction in the former Westside Pavilion shopping center in West Los Angeles on Aug. 19, 2024
( Brian van der Brug,
/
Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today (https://support.laist.com/quick-donate?ms=prenote&utm_source=laist&utm_medium=onsite_prenote&utm_campaign=prenote&utm_content=control_v1).
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1) obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
More news
The Supreme Court rejects a DOJ push to separate California ballots (https://laist.com/news/politics/the-supreme-court-rejects-a-doj-push-to-separate-california-ballots)
The U.S. Supreme Court has denied a last-minute request from the Department of Justice to wade into its unprecedented feud with California over the state's voter rolls.
What we know so far about LA and OC voter turnout in the 2026 midterm election (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-midterm-voter-turnout-los-angeles-orange-county)
A look at how many showed up to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, either in person or by mail, and how it compares to previous elections.
Beware the ‘red mirage’ if California Republicans have an election night lead (https://laist.com/news/politics/red-mirage-california-republicans-election-night-lead)
Don’t be fooled by early election returns. It can take California weeks to tally votes, leading to ‘red mirages’ and ‘blue shifts.’
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
Sponsored message
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they're well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
Sponsored message
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn't answer CalMatters' questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
Mazziotta also told the regents the institute's construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. 2. **The institute is explicitly exempt from California's transparency and ethics laws.** Verified in §130363(a): "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law, including... Division 10 (commencing with Section 7920.000) [California Public Records Act], Article 9 (commencing with Section 11120) [Brown Act open meetings], and Title 9 (commencing with Section 81000) [Political Reform Act]."
   
   So $4.2B in taxpayer money goes to a private nonprofit that is statutorily exempt from public records, open meetings, and conflict-of-interest/financial-disclosure rules. The pro argument claims "strong accountability including independent audits" — audits exist, but they are financial audits by a CPA the institute itself commissions (§130361(a)), reviewed by the Controller. That is not a substitute for CPRA/Brown Act/Political Reform Act. And UC's own general counsel could not tell the Regents where the line is between public and private documents, given four senior UCLA officials sit on CIII's board.

3. **The institute doesn't functionally exist yet.** As of Sept 2026 UC Regents testimony from UCLA Health CEO John Mazziotta: 3 employees (a COO, general counsel, and a scientific advisor), still searching for a director, only ~$20M spent vs. a plan calling for $45M operating + $167M capital, construction costs underfunded by ~$100M, facility not complete until late 2028. State filings from May 2026 showed zero employees. Meanwhile §130353(e)(1) immediately appropriates a **$100 million General Fund start-up loan** to the institute on the effective date — before any bonds are even sold.

4. **The institute gets control over everyone else's IP.** §130358(e)(2): the institute "shall serve as a clearinghouse and approval center for ALL agreements to sell, license, or otherwise commercialize or monetize intellectual property rights that arise from research funded under this chapter." §130358(e)(2)(C): when the institute participates, it "shall have the primary responsibility for negotiating any agreement for the sale, licensing, or other commercialization." §130357(d)-(e): every grant recipient must offer the institute the opportunity to "substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer **UCLA by name** the same for clinical trials. §130356(e)(2): the council "shall confer with the institute... in making final decisions regarding the funding of grant proposals."
   
   So the "competitive" half isn't competitive: grants go only to institutions "represented on the council" (§130352(b)(2)) — a self-selected closed pool of 7 UC campuses plus 10-15 members those 7 appoint — UC Merced, UC Santa Barbara, UC Santa Cruz, Cal State, community colleges, and any non-council institution are all shut out. The council's first chair is statutorily the UCLA representative (§130355(d)(2)). And the pre-selected institute has a veto-adjacent role in both grant decisions and all commercialization.

5. **Conflict-of-interest rules are weakened, not strengthened.** §130363(b)(1): council members "may participate in a decision to approve or award a grant or contract to an entity in the same field as their employer." §130363(b)(2): they may participate in decisions involving "a disease from which the member or a person in their family suffers." §130363(d): Government Code §1090 — California's core criminal anti-self-dealing statute — "shall not apply" to council grants except in a narrow two-part case. For a measure whose proponents tout "rigorous conflict of interest rules," this is the opposite.

6. **The pro argument's fiscal claims are false.** The official Yes argument says the measure is "Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers." The Legislative Analyst's official estimate says the opposite: $500-600M/yr for ~20 years from the General Fund, ~10% more than paying cash (after inflation), and revenue offsets are "uncertain" and "could take decades." The debt is legally guaranteed; the royalties are speculative.
   
   And we have a 20-year natural experiment: Prop 71 (2004) and Prop 14 (2020) — $8.5B in nearly identical "self-repaying" research bonds with the same royalty-return structure. CIRM's audited financials show the Stem Cell Licensing Revenue and Royalties Fund took in **$677,205** in FY2024 against hundreds of millions in annual debt service. Two decades in, essentially zero of the bond cost has been recovered. The same promise is being made again, with the same architecture.

7. **The "20% Rx discount" is close to meaningless as advertised.** Verified in §130358(b): the discount applies only to "a technology or drug developed through research funded pursuant to this chapter" — i.e., only drugs arising from this specific $8.4B program, which realistically will be a handful of products at most, decades out. It is not a general prescription drug discount for Californians. Presenting it as a headline benefit ("Mandates 20% Rx discount") in the ballot argument is materially misleading.

8. **It's the wrong instrument and there's a better one already in the pipeline.** Bonds are for long-lived capital assets (roads, buildings, water). Using 20-year general obligation debt to fund operating research grants means paying interest on salaries and reagents. And SB 895 (Wiener), signed by Newsom, already puts a **$7.5 billion** scientific research bond on the **March 2028** ballot — broad, multi-field, peer-reviewed, competitively awarded, with transparency protections. That is 16 months away. Opponent Robert Kaplan (former NIH associate director) specifically says SB 895 "has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect." Voting No on 38 doesn't kill research funding; it clears the way for a better-designed version.

9. **The process is corrupted by a ~6,000-to-1 money gap.** Yes: $71,229,216 (through 10/22/26), of which ~$61.2M is Michelson/Michelson Center — with ~$14M structured as *loans* from Michelson. No: $11,990. Nearly $20M spent on TV ads, $10M+ on signature gathering. The opposition is literally a letter-writing campaign funded by ~$12 thousand. When one side outspends the other 6,000:1 and the measure's largest donor is the chair of its largest beneficiary, the 57% poll support is a function of advertising, not informed consent.

10. **Near-unanimous informed opposition.** 12 editorial boards: SF Chronicle ("one of the most noxious deposits on California's political dung heap in years"), Sacramento Bee/McClatchy California, Mercury News/East Bay Times ("an $8.4 billion money grab"), LA Times (George Skelton: No), San Diego Union-Tribune, Orange County Register, Press Democrat, Santa Cruz Sentinel, Bakersfield Californian, Santa Barbara Independent, Daily Californian, Bay Area Reporter, SF Bay Guardian. Organizations spanning left and right: League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, Consumer Watchdog, Courage California, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, DSA (SF, LA, California, Inland Empire), ACCE Action, Peace and Freedom Party, GrowSF, LA Forward, Knock LA. Plus three former Legislative Analysts (Marianne O'Malley, Judy Heiman, Dan Carson) and a former NIH associate director.
    
    The Yes side has real support — Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Association, ALS Association, Kidney Cancer Association, American Nurses Association California, American Association of Immunologists, both state parties, Newsom. But notably: patient advocacy groups are being courted by a $71M ad campaign invoking cancer and Alzheimer's; several cancer survivors and patients are themselves leading the opposition, saying their illnesses are being "exploited to shill for an initiative that is overly narrow, opaque and expensive." And the UC itself — whose name is invoked throughout — took **no position**.

**Possible counterarguments for Yes, honestly weighed:**
- Federal NIH funding is genuinely being cut/destabilized by the Trump administration, and California research is suffering. Real problem. But Prop 38 doesn't address it broadly — it addresses one subfield and one institute, and SB 895 addresses it properly in 16 months.
- Immunotherapy is genuinely promising (CAR-T, checkpoint inhibitors). True. But that's an argument for funding immunology through peer review across all California institutions — which is what the SB 895 bond does — not for handing half to a 3-employee nonprofit exempt from the Public Records Act.
- The 10% royalty clawback and 20% price discount are good ideas in principle. But the CIRM precedent shows the clawback returns pennies, and the discount applies only to this program's own future drugs.
- $500-600M/yr is only ~0.25% of the General Fund. True — but it's a continuous appropriation (§130379) that competes directly with Medi-Cal, schools, housing and wildfire response for two decades, in a state with structural deficits, and it's *incremental* to the existing CIRM debt service Californians already pay (~$587M+/yr).
- Audits and annual reports exist. True, but financial audits ≠ public records/open meetings/conflict-of-interest law. And the measure affirmatively strips all three.

**Bottom line.** The policy goal is legitimate. The instrument is not. This measure takes a sympathetic cause — curing cancer and Alzheimer's — and uses it to move $4.2 billion of taxpayer money into a private nonprofit that (a) is not named in the text voters see, (b) was written to be uniquely eligible via criteria matching its own founder's donations almost verbatim, (c) is chaired by the measure's chief funder, (d) had 3 employees and no director as of two months before the election, (e) is statutorily exempt from the Public Records Act, Brown Act, and Political Reform Act, (f) gets approval authority over all other grantees' IP and commercialization, and (g) is financed by a 6,000:1 spending advantage while the official Yes argument tells voters it costs taxpayers nothing, contrary to the Legislative Analyst's own estimate — a claim California already tested for 20 years with CIRM and got back $677 thousand.

Voting No does not oppose medical research. It opposes this deal. And a better-designed $7.5B research bond is already on the March 2028 ballot.
